clue.text: Blind's said to be what these spirits make you

definitions.note: Americans call window blinds by this name

blocks.note: first meaning: in American usage window blinds are known by this word
second meaning: ghosts; the surface plays on strong drink making you blind drunk

explanation.surface: A drinker is warned that a few stiff spirits will leave them blind drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: The spirits are not drink but ghosts, and the blind is a window covering, as Americans name it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ghosts of the dead were called by this word in classical poetry, and in American English a roller blind goes by the same word.

clue.text: Transport lobby should be listened to!

indicators.note: something to be listened to is heard rather than read, so the word's sound counts, not its spelling

blocks.note: a hall is an entrance lobby

explanation.surface: A transport lobby group demands that politicians listen to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lobby' looks like a pressure group but is the entrance room of a house.
explanation.definitionFit: To drag or carry goods, usually heavy loads by lorry, is a verb sense of moving them from place to place.

clue.text: One advancing argument should make it stand up

indicators.note: the letters that follow are made into something new, rearranged into another word

blocks.note: the three words taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: Whoever puts forward an argument ought to make sure it holds up under scrutiny.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone engaged in a dispute puts forward contentions, so a debater advancing a case is exactly this kind of person.

clue.text: Peg for toper putting away one good short after another

indicators.note: a drinker putting away a dram takes it inside, so one word is swallowed by another

blocks.note: a toper and a sot are both habitual drunkards
a greedy guzzler who downs drink after drink is a hog or glutton

explanation.surface: A heavy drinker downs one small measure of spirits after another.
explanation.walkthrough: A short is a small measure of spirits; one who downs them one after another greedily is a glutton, held inside the drunkard to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A tap or plug stopping a cask is a wooden peg, so the word for that stopper fits.

clue.text: Cruel, cold one with no heart, say - totally reactionary

indicators.note: reactionary means turned back, so the whole string of pieces is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for cold on a tap
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
a heart is one example of a playing card

explanation.surface: A heartless, cold and cruel person is painted as an utter reactionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No heart' reads as heartlessness, but the heart is a playing card.
explanation.definitionFit: Draco's ancient Athenian law code was notoriously severe, so his name gives an adjective for harsh, cruel punishment.

clue.text: Play resulting in risky free kick

blocks.note: risky and perilous mean the same
a corner is a kick awarded in football

explanation.surface: A dangerous piece of football play earns the opposition a free kick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' looks like a football move, but it is a stage drama by J.B. Priestley.
explanation.definitionFit: Priestley wrote this 1932 stage drama about a dinner party whose chance remark exposes buried secrets.

clue.text: These attacks will deploy Stealth - US President's spoken!

definitions.note: a description of the answer rather than a synonym

indicators.note: something spoken is heard, so the sound of the words counts rather than their spelling

blocks.note: in 2001 the President was George W. Bush, who might introduce himself 'I am Bush'

explanation.surface: Air strikes using Stealth bombers are announced after the American President has spoken.
explanation.walkthrough: The President in 2001 was Bush; heard aloud as the President's own words, 'am Bush's' gives the answer. Stealth suggests the bomber, but surprise attacks need stealth.
explanation.definitionFit: Attacks launched by surprise from a hidden position depend on stealth, which is the essence of the answer.

clue.text: Pound note - formerly sovereign

blocks.note: once means at one time in the past
R stands for rex or regina, king or queen

explanation.surface: The pound note, like the old gold sovereign coin, belongs to Britain's monetary past.
explanation.walkthrough: A sovereign was also a gold pound coin, which feeds the money surface, but here it means the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Old British slang called the one-pound banknote by this name, withdrawn from circulation in England in 1988.

clue.text: Take-off gives one a funny feeling

blocks.note: first meaning: a comic imitation of someone
second meaning: a vague notion or hunch

explanation.surface: An aircraft taking off leaves a passenger with an odd sensation in the stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take-off' suggests flight, but it is a mimic's comic imitation.
explanation.definitionFit: A comedian's imitation of a celebrity is called this, and so is a vague hunch or notion that something is so.

clue.text: Quiz shows matter!

blocks.note: first meaning: to interrogate someone
second meaning: an issue under discussion

explanation.surface: Television quiz shows are important, it is claimed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quiz shows' reads as television programmes; 'Quiz' is a verb, and 'shows' merely joins it to the second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: To interrogate a suspect is a verb sense, and an issue up for debate, as in 'the matter in hand', is the noun sense.

clue.text: Power evident in blue's muscles

indicators.note: something evident in a thing is seen within it, so one letter sits inside the other word

blocks.note: bice is a pale blue pigment, with the S of the possessive
P is the symbol for power in physics

explanation.surface: A sportsman's strength shows in his muscles.
explanation.walkthrough: Bice is an obscure blue or green pigment used by painters.
explanation.definitionFit: The two-headed muscles at the front of the upper arm are named from the Latin for two heads.

clue.text: In an area of special interest near home?

definitions.text: In an area of special interest near home?

blocks.clueFragment: In an area of special interest
blocks.note: surface reading: a district designated for its special interest, like a conservation zone
setter's reading: a road beside your own house, which is the idiom for something that suits your tastes

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like planning jargon; the idiom literally places a thing on the road where you live.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something that matches one's own interests or abilities, pictured as lying on the road outside home.

clue.text: Exam to get through - failure would make one cast down

indicators.note: getting through something means passing within it, so one word goes inside another

blocks.note: a demise is a collapse or end
an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: A student must pass a test, since failing it would leave them dejected.
explanation.definitionFit: To dishearten someone and sap their confidence is to leave them dejected and low in spirits.

clue.text: Pour the tea on reaching platform?

blocks.note: the British phrase 'be mother' means pour the tea, so to pour is to be
the one who pours the tea is 'mother', shortened to ma

explanation.surface: Someone serves tea on arriving at a station platform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shall I be mother?' is a British teatime phrase meaning 'Shall I pour?'; with mother as MA it splits into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised speaker's stand, in ancient Athens or a synagogue, is called by this Greek word for step.

clue.text: Sort of pit to supply capstone material

indicators.note: raw material is worked into a new form, so the preceding letters are reworked into another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A quarry is dug to provide stone for the top of a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Surface mining scrapes away the ground without tunnels, giving a kind of mine worked in the open.

clue.text: Very little money distresses utterly Dome's supporters

indicators.note: uttered means spoken, so the word before is to be heard rather than read

blocks.note: a cent is a coin of tiny value
to wring someone's heart is to distress them

explanation.surface: A shortage of cash causes total distress to those backing the Millennium Dome.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dome was London's troubled Millennium Dome, which kept needing money; 'utterly' looks like 'totally' but means said aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Builders put up temporary timber frameworks to hold an arch or vault while it sets, and these props carry a dome too.

clue.text: Fail to catch properly, so rugby player awarded try

blocks.note: a scrum half or fly half
a judge tries a case, that is, hears it

explanation.surface: A rugby player misses the ball, yet the referee still gives his team a try.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch' and 'try' both look like rugby, but the catching is listening and the try is a court hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearing only part of what is said means missing words, so one does not quite catch a remark.

clue.text: Armed robbers traced to bottom flats

blocks.note: the foot of a page is its bottom
a pad is slang for a flat or home

explanation.surface: Police trace a gang of armed robbers to a basement block of flats.
explanation.definitionFit: Highway thieves who went on foot rather than on horseback were the old name for muggers who robbed travellers.

clue.text: Time for the daily dozen?

blocks.note: surface reading: the moment to do one's daily set of keep-fit exercises
setter's reading: the dozen is the hour of twelve on the clock each day

explanation.walkthrough: The daily dozen is a routine of twelve exercises, but here it is twelve o'clock in the day.
explanation.definitionFit: Twelve o'clock in the middle of the day comes once daily, and is the twelfth hour reached by the clock.

clue.text: Late developer

blocks.note: first meaning: previous, as in 'the late chairman'
second meaning: one who forms or shapes something

explanation.walkthrough: 'Late developer' is a familiar phrase for a slow-maturing child; split it into two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Late' can mean previous or ex, and a person who shapes or creates things is one who forms them.

clue.text: Royal attendant's a tart

blocks.note: first meaning: an unmarried lady attending a queen or princess
second meaning: a small British pastry with an almond or curd filling

explanation.surface: A scandal: the queen's lady-in-waiting is a woman of loose morals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tart' looks like the slang insult, but it is a small cake, Richmond's famous almond-curd pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: An unmarried noblewoman serving a queen has this title, and a Richmond pastry tartlet shares the same name.

clue.text: A cracking thump meant to intimidate

indicators.note: a letter cracking something breaks into it, so it ends up lodged inside the other word

blocks.note: dunt is a Scottish and northern word for a heavy blow
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hard punch is thrown purely to frighten someone.
explanation.walkthrough: Dunt is a dialect word, chiefly Scottish, for a dull heavy blow.
explanation.definitionFit: To dishearten or make someone afraid is to frighten them off, which is the sense of the verb.

clue.text: Bats stood to hit for six

indicators.note: in a down clue a word that stood up is read from the bottom upward

blocks.note: bats and nuts both mean crazy

explanation.surface: The cricket bats were stood ready for the batsman to hit a six.
explanation.walkthrough: To hit for six is British idiom, from cricket, for to stagger or astonish someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Being knocked for six means being shocked or stunned, so the idiom is a synonym for astonish.

clue.text: Precise moment

blocks.note: first meaning: very detailed, pronounced my-NEWT
second meaning: a brief space of time

explanation.walkthrough: 'Precise moment' reads as one phrase; split it into an adjective and a noun, pronounced differently.
explanation.definitionFit: A painstakingly detailed account is described with this adjective, while the noun means sixty seconds or a very short time.

clue.text: Propose to girl in short letter

indicators.note: something placed in another thing sits inside it, so the name goes within the other word

blocks.note: a note is a brief letter
Mina is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A shy suitor proposes marriage to his girlfriend in a brief letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Propose to girl' suggests marriage; here propose means put forward a candidate.
explanation.definitionFit: To put someone forward as a candidate for office or an award is to name them formally.

clue.text: Change direction to take another turn for the better?

indicators.note: another version of the word is a different arrangement of its letters
the outer word takes the other in, holding it within itself

blocks.note: to veer is to swerve
taken as written

explanation.surface: A patient's condition shifts course, hoping to take a turn for the better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn for the better' is a set phrase, but 'better' here is one who bets, punning on bettor.
explanation.definitionFit: A gambler who places a wager takes a risk, and anyone who risks money on a chance is a speculator of this kind.

clue.text: Doctor dresses evil swelling

indicators.note: something that dresses another clothes it, wrapping around the outside

blocks.note: to doctor results is to rig or fix them
sin is wickedness

explanation.surface: A doctor puts a dressing on a nasty swelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' and 'dresses' suggest medicine, but the doctor is a fixer and the dressing is a wrapping.
explanation.definitionFit: A lump or bump that rises up from the skin is a swelling, the noun sense of the word.
